name: Creature Keywords
content:
Every stat block lists one or more **creature keywords**. A keyword means nothing on its own, but abilities, treasures, and Malice features often key off them — a creature with the Goblin keyword, for example, can benefit from and contribute to goblin Malice features. Some keywords name a specific family (Gnoll, Human); others are broad tags for a creature's origin or nature, shared across many groups. The common general keywords are:

- **Abyssal** — Traces back to the Abyssal Wasteland, a chaotic manifold whose denizens crave mortal souls (demons, gnolls).
- **Accursed** — Reshaped by a powerful supernatural curse (medusas, werewolves).
- **Animal** — Natural creatures with animal-level minds and only natural defenses (bears, wolves, oversized spiders).
- **Beast** — Animal-level minds paired with supernatural traits (basilisks, chimeras).
- **Construct** — Built and animated by magic or psionics; sapience depends on the maker. Needs no food, water, sleep, or air unless noted.
- **Dragon** — Dragons and their kin, such as draconians.
- **Elemental** — Origin traced to Quintessence, the Manifold of Elements.
- **Fey** — Origin in Arcadia, the manifold of nature and magic; often innately tied to nature, magic, or both.
- **Giant** — Humanoid-shaped but far larger (ogres, trolls, and the various giants); unrelated to most humanoids, the hakaan aside.
- **Horror** — Alien, unnatural creatures, frequently strongly psionic (overminds, voiceless talkers).
- **Humanoid** — Size 1 creatures with human-like limbs and sapience who tend to build communities.
- **Infernal** — Traces back to the Seven Cities of Hell, where natives bargain for mortal souls (devils, hobgoblins).
- **Ooze** — Semisolid masses that gather in dark, damp places (the gummy brick).
- **Plant** — Living vegetation that can move and act, unlike inert plant objects (the shambling mound).
- **Swarm** — Many small creatures that move and act together as a single creature.
- **Undead** — Reanimated dead whose sapience depends on what raised them. Needs no food, water, sleep, or air unless noted.

name: Reading a Stat Block
content:
Most of a creature's stat block reads like a hero's traits and abilities. A few Director-facing details are worth calling out:

**Languages.** A creature's lore includes a Languages entry only if it speaks at least one language.

**Keywords.** Each block lists one or more [creature keywords](#creature-keywords).

**Encounter Value (EV).** Every Director-run creature has an EV used to budget encounters (see [Building Encounters](#building-encounters)).

**Combat rounds.** Any mention of "rounds" in a stat block means combat rounds.

**Free strikes.** A creature's free strike deals a fixed value with no roll. It reaches melee 1 (or the melee distance of the creature's signature ability, whichever is greater) or ranged 5 (or the signature ability's ranged distance, whichever is greater). It gains the Strike keyword, plus Magic, Psionic, or Weapon if the signature ability has them, and uses the signature ability's damage type — your choice when there's more than one. Static values keep play fast and let heroes weigh the risk of provoking one.

**Opportunity attacks.** Even though free strikes don't roll, a creature that has a bane on strikes against a target can't make an opportunity attack against that target.

**Self-reference.** When a stat block says "enemies," "allies," or "within X squares," it means relative to that creature unless the text says otherwise.

**Signature ability.** A creature's first listed action, marked Signature Ability.

**Traits.** Always-on features that need no action to use.

**Malice.** Some abilities cost the Director's [Malice](#malice) to activate.

**End effect.** Some creatures can take unpreventable damage to end one effect on them that a saving throw could end.

name: Villain Actions
content:
Solo and leader creatures are built for climactic battles, and they back that up with **villain actions**. A creature with villain actions always has exactly three. Each can be used once per encounter, and no more than one villain action can be used per round (even with two such creatures in play, which should be rare).

A villain action triggers at the end of any other creature's turn. They're numbered to suggest a dramatic arc, but you may use them in any order:

- **First — the opener.** A statement that this is no ordinary foe. Openers tend to deal some damage, summon lackeys, buff the villain, debuff the heroes, or reposition the villain to advantage.
- **Second — crowd control.** Usually deployed once the heroes have responded and surrounded the villain. Stronger than the opener, it helps the villain seize back the initiative.
- **Third — the ultimate.** A showstopper that lands a devastating blow before the fight ends.

name: Creature Organization
content:
A creature's **organization** appears after its level and sets its power and encounter value — a level 1 ghoul is not as strong as a level 1 orc. Some families field many weak creatures; others field a few formidable ones. A creature may use one main organization plus a few minions, or mix several types.

- **Minion.** Weak foes made to die fast and threaten in numbers, built four at a time. They support other monsters and follow special squad rules (see [Using Minions](#using-minions)).
- **Horde.** Hardier than minions but still reliant on numbers — roughly two per equal-level hero. They're fragile, so double or triple them up when they matter.
- **Platoon.** Organized, self-sufficient, and well-rounded — about one per hero, often joined by minions and an elite or two.
- **Elite.** The opposite of minions: a single elite can stand against two equal-level heroes and carries a high EV. Several elites can fight together as a band.
- **Leader.** A powerful monster who buffs allies and grants them extra actions, wields [villain actions](#villain-actions), and can take on two or more equal-level heroes alone. Usually only one appears per battle, and a leader has no separate [role](#creature-roles).
- **Solo.** An entire encounter by itself, with special rules in its stat block. A solo can face about six equal-level heroes and has no separate role.

name: Creature Roles
content:
A creature's **role** appears after its level and organization and describes its job in a fight. Roles are descriptive — most carry no special rules — but they help you assemble encounters and play creatures to their strengths.

- **Ambusher.** Melee fighters who slip past the front line to reach softer targets in the back.
- **Artillery.** Fights best from a distance, landing its strongest abilities far away.
- **Brute.** High Stamina and damage; hard to ignore, hard to escape, and good at shoving foes around.
- **Controller.** Reshapes the battlefield, often with magic or psionics — repositioning foes and altering terrain. Usually fragile, so it needs protection.
- **Defender.** A tough damage-soaker who can force foes to attack it instead of squishier allies.
- **Harrier.** A mobile hit-and-run fighter who makes the most of positioning.
- **Hexer.** A debuff specialist who stacks conditions and effects. Squishy, and reliant on others for cover.
- **Mount.** A mobile creature meant to be ridden, making its rider more dangerous.
- **Support.** Aids allies with buffs, healing, movement, or extra options.

name: Special Creature Rules
content:
A few general rules cover creatures who take certain actions:

**Defending.** A creature that has already taken a main action this turn can't also take the Defend main action — even if it's granted an extra main action — unless it's specifically allowed to Defend.

**Grabbing.** Unless its stat block says otherwise, a creature can keep only one creature or object grabbed at a time. To grab another target with that ability, it must first release one.

**Summoning.** Unless noted, a summoned creature or object acts immediately after its summoner. A creature that summons can't summon again until the start of its next turn.

**Healing via damage.** When an ability lets a creature regain Stamina equal to the damage it deals and that ability hits several targets, the creature regains Stamina from only one instance of the damage — not the combined total.

name: Malice
content:
Just as each hero has a Heroic Resource, the Director has **Malice** — the fuel that lets monsters unleash their strongest abilities and spring surprises mid-combat.

### Earning Malice

At the start of combat, gain Malice equal to the average number of Victories per hero. At the start of each combat round, gain Malice equal to the number of heroes in the fight plus the current round number.

For example, five heroes with 3 Victories each begin round 1 with **9 Malice** — 3 for the average Victories, 5 for the heroes, and 1 for the round. As long as every hero stays in the fight, that's **7** in round 2, **8** in round 3, **9** in round 4, and so on. A hero who dies stops generating Malice, and any unused Malice is lost at the encounter's end. Whether you reveal your Malice total to the players is up to you — the slow climb can build great tension, or the mystery can keep them guessing.

### Spending Malice

Monsters spend Malice the way heroes spend their Heroic Resource: to activate and enhance abilities whose Malice cost is noted in the stat block. Some creature types also have a once-per-turn option listed in a "[Creature] Malice" entry that precedes their stat blocks, usually affecting a whole group of enemies, granting extra actions, or changing the environment. You'll never afford everything — spend on small effects each round, hoard for a dramatic moment, or repeat one feature. Do whatever's most fun and fits the scene.

### Basic Malice features

Every monster can use these in addition to any creature-specific Malice features. At the start of any monster's turn, you may spend:

- **Brutal Effectiveness (3 Malice).** The next ability the monster uses that has a potency increases that potency by 1.
- **Malicious Strike (5+ Malice).** The monster's next strike deals extra damage to one target equal to its highest characteristic score, plus 1 more for each additional Malice spent (to a maximum of three times that characteristic). This feature can't be used two rounds in a row, even by different monsters.

> **Prep tip.** You usually need only three Malice features ready for an encounter — four if you're mixing monster types or bands. Pick one costing 2–3 Malice, one costing 5, and one costing 7–10, and you're covered.

name: Using Minions
content:
Minions are weak alone but dangerous in numbers, and because they fight as units rather than individuals they follow a few special rules. None of it is secret — share it with your players so everyone enjoys carving through the horde.

**Squads.** Minions that share a name (for example, *goblin sniper*) form a **squad** of up to eight. The whole squad shares one place in initiative and acts together.

**Shared Stamina pool.** A squad's Stamina is a single pool equal to one minion's Stamina times the number of minions in the squad. Damage to any minion comes off the pool. Minions can't be winded, can't regain Stamina, and can't gain temporary Stamina.

**Losing minions.** Each time the pool drops by one minion's Stamina, one minion is removed — first whoever took the hit, then the nearest. A single non-area hit large enough to cover two or more minions' Stamina drops that many at once (the target first, then outward to the nearest); let the player narrate the carnage.

| Damage to the pool | Minions left |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 8 |
| 5 | 7 |
| 10 | 6 |
| 15 | 5 |
| 20 | 4 |
| 25 | 3 |
| 30 | 2 |
| 35 | 1 |
| 40 | 0 |

*A squad of eight goblin spinecleavers (5 Stamina each) has a 40-point pool; every 5 damage removes one minion.*

**Area effects.** An area ability damages the pool once for each minion it actually catches, but it can only remove minions standing in the area — never more than were hit.

**Weakness & immunity.** If the minions have a damage weakness or immunity, apply it to the squad once (even when every minion shares it), as the final step of the damage calculation.

**Acting together.** On the squad's turn the minions act in concert. When several use their signature ability, make one roll for the whole squad. Each target is affected once; when two or three minions strike the *same* target, each extra minion adds its free-strike value as bonus damage — so it is usually better to spread attacks across different heroes. A critical hit on the squad's signature ability lets every participating minion take another main action.

**Action economy.** Each minion gets a move action plus a main action, a move plus a maneuver, or two moves. Minions can take opportunity attacks but rarely have other triggered actions.

**Maneuvers.** A squad performs Grab, Hide, Knockback, and Search as a unit — one roll, each target affected once. A minion may instead take another maneuver on its own (usually to stand up or escape a grab), but then it sits out the squad's shared action that turn.

**Combined free strikes.** When several minions in a squad free strike the same target at once, total their damage and treat it as a single strike.

**Tracking squads.** Running two squads of the same minion? Mark them — different minis, colored rings, or VTT tints — so everyone can tell which minion belongs to which squad.

name: Captains
content:
Any creature that isn't a mount or a minion, and that speaks a language a squad of minions understands, can attach to that squad as its **captain**. Captains aren't always clever tacticians — some simply bully, inspire, or supernaturally compel the minions to act. A squad can have only one captain, and a creature can captain only one squad.

**Separate actions and Stamina.** A captain takes its turn alongside its squad but isn't bound by the minions' action limits. Its Stamina is tracked on its own and never joins the squad's pool.

**Benefits.** While a squad has a captain, every minion in it gains the bonus listed at the "With Captain" entry on its stat block — commonly extra damage, more speed, or additional Stamina.

**Replacing a captain.** If a squad loses its captain, another allied creature can become captain at the start of the next round, no action required.

name: Stat Block Icons
content:
The printed stat blocks use small icons for quick scanning. On this site the same information is spelled out in plain labels and pills, so you won't need a key to read an ability. For reference, the markers a stat block distinguishes are:

- **Distance** of an ability.
- **Targets** or affected area.
- **Trait** — a feature that's always in effect.
- **Melee** ability.
- **Ranged** ability.
- **Melee or ranged** — your choice.
- **Self** — an ability that affects only the user.
- **Area (cube, line, or wall).**
- **Area (aura or burst).**
- **Special** — a unique distance, often the whole encounter map.
- **Triggered action.**
- **Leader/solo feature**, such as a villain action.

name: Building Encounters
content:
An encounter is a scene that puts the heroes against a challenge or opposition. These guidelines focus on combat encounters. Treat them as a starting point — the heroes' builds, the map, their treasures, the dice, and tactical skill all sway the result, so expect to fine-tune for your group.

### Step 1: Think

A strong encounter usually has a backstory or inciting incident, interesting monsters, a reason for everyone to be there, stakes for failure, at least one chance for the heroes and their foes to learn something, and a map that rewards teamwork.

### Step 2: Choose a difficulty

- **Trivial.** No real challenge; the heroes are never in danger. Usually earns no Victory.
- **Easy.** Won't threaten the heroes' lives unless they're already depleted. Worth 1 Victory.
- **Standard.** The common case; drains some Stamina and Recoveries, and a bad turn can be deadly. Worth 1 Victory.
- **Hard.** Often a climactic fight that puts lives in real peril, but winnable with smart play. Worth 2 Victories.
- **Extreme.** Likely lethal if the heroes fight to the bitter end; rare in most campaigns. Worth 2 or more Victories.

### Step 3: Determine Encounter Strength

Each hero's **encounter strength (ES)** is 4, plus 2 per level — so a 3rd-level hero has an ES of 10. Add every hero's ES together for the party's ES (five 3rd-level heroes = 50). A retainer or allied NPC counts as a hero of its level. For every 2 Victories the heroes have earned on average, raise the party's ES as though it had one more hero.

| Hero level | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1st | 6 | 12 | 18 | 24 | 30 | 36 | 42 | 48 |
| 2nd | 8 | 16 | 24 | 32 | 40 | 48 | 56 | 64 |
| 3rd | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 | 70 | 80 |
| 4th | 12 | 24 | 36 | 48 | 60 | 72 | 84 | 96 |
| 5th | 14 | 28 | 42 | 56 | 70 | 84 | 98 | 112 |
| 6th | 16 | 32 | 48 | 64 | 80 | 96 | 112 | 128 |
| 7th | 18 | 36 | 54 | 72 | 90 | 108 | 126 | 144 |
| 8th | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 | 100 | 120 | 140 | 160 |
| 9th | 22 | 44 | 66 | 88 | 110 | 132 | 154 | 176 |
| 10th | 24 | 48 | 72 | 96 | 120 | 144 | 168 | 192 |

*Columns are the number of heroes. Add one hero for every 2 Victories earned on average.*

### Step 4: Set the budget

Spend encounter value on monsters up to a budget set by the difficulty, measured against the party's ES (call one hero's ES a "share"):

- **Trivial** — less than the party ES minus one share.
- **Easy** — less than the party ES, but above the trivial budget.
- **Standard** — between the party ES and the party ES plus one share.
- **Hard** — above standard, up to the party ES plus three shares.
- **Extreme** — anything above the hard budget.

> **Pacing.** Most groups can handle 4–6 Victories' worth of combat before needing a respite, and combat encounters should carry real narrative weight — a quick scuffle with two bumbling guards is better resolved with a test than a full battle.
